extracted.intended_audience: poets, dramatists, and literary critics (writers and readers of poetry and drama)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for composing and defending poetry/drama and for answering critics — covers choice of subject, diction, use of ornament, modes of imitation, and how to reconcile apparent faults in poetic works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reserve ornaments for weak places
rubrics_metrics.description: All those places which are either absurd or weak, and that cannot maintain themselves, ought to be supported by all the Ornaments of the Diction; as Homer, Virgil, Demosthenes and Cicero have happily practiced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use rhetorical ornamentation (elegant diction, comparisons, descriptive passages) to cover or support parts of the fable that would otherwise seem absurd or weak. Example: Homer surrounds the implausible device of Ulysses sleeping ashore with many admirable descriptive passages so the reader is 'enchanted' and does not perceive the defect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ornament where good sentiment or manners suffice
rubrics_metrics.description: Those that have either good Sentiments or Manners, have no occasion for [ornaments]; a good Sentiment never appears better than in a simple Style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the content is morally weighty or exhibits character/manners, prefer plainness; ornamentation would obscure the thought. Hermogenes: moral writing should be plain and without artifice.

rubrics_metrics.name: A brilliant expression can damage sentiment and manners
rubrics_metrics.description: A brilliant, or glorious expression damages them rather, and serves only to hide their beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bombastic or lofty style is contrary to the depiction of manners and sentiment; avoid florid language when it would conceal character or moral truths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use ornament only to serve poetic ends, not to excuse sloppiness
rubrics_metrics.description: An absurdity in the fable ceases to be a fault when by those means the poet obtains the end he proposed; but if the same end can be obtained without infringing the rules of art, the fault is less pardonable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ornament may legitimately hide or justify an implausible device only if it produces a necessary effect (e.g., astonishment, wonder) that could not be achieved otherwise; but poets should avoid relying on such devices when avoidable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select subjects within the poet's capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: Be sure all you that undertake to write, to choose a Subject for your Genius fit; try long and often what your Talents are, what your parts will bear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A chief fault is choosing subjects above one's power; poets should test their capacity and select arguments and burdens their talents can sustain. (Horace quoted.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate intrinsic (proper) faults from accidental (foreign) faults
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two defects in Poetry: one that proceeds from itself (proper), and the other which happens by Accident (foreign). When it chooses Subjects out of its reach and power, 'tis that which proceeds from itself; but when it chooses subjects that are not above it, but vicious, this is that which happens by Accident.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intrinsic faults (faulty imitation, bad choice of subject) are more serious and less excusable; faults arising from ignorance of other arts (anatomy, geography, medicine) are accidental and more pardonable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not judge poetry by political or non-poetic standards
rubrics_metrics.description: We must remember that we should not judge of the Excellence of Poetry as of Politics, nor as of any other of the Arts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each art has its own ends — poetry aims at imitation and evoking effects (e.g., wonder, pity), not at fulfilling rules of statecraft or medicine. Criticisms based on other arts' standards are often unjust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes of imitation: represent as it was, as it is, or as it ought to be
rubrics_metrics.description: He represents a Subject either as it was, or as it is, or such as it ought to be; and to do that, he uses either proper or foreign Words, or Metaphors, or any of the other Manners of Diction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When defending imitation choices, show whether the poet meant to depict reality, report, or an idealized/ought-to-be version. Different genres may favor different modes (epic/tragedy: as ought to be; comedy: as it is).

rubrics_metrics.name: Permit poetic liberties in diction and expression
rubrics_metrics.description: The Poets have the liberty to employ proper or foreign Words, Metaphors, or any other Manners of Diction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When critics attack diction, examine whether the poet used allowable poetic devices (metaphor, foreign usage, archaic forms). Such liberties can justify departures from ordinary speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal to custom, report or fame as a valid defense
rubrics_metrics.description: We must have recourse to Fame, and demonstrate that she hath said so; and the Authority of Custom is often used to defend the Poets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an expression reflects common report, customary usage, or widespread belief (e.g., local variants, traditional stories), that can justify the poet's choice. Examples: local claims about Ulysses' marriage, customary naming or practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolve apparent faults by examining alternate meanings, pointing, or accent
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes we have recourse to the Ambiguity, or to the different pointing; in changing the Accent we find a different and defensible sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apparent errors or contradictions may be resolved by reading words in alternate senses, by shifting accent or punctuation (pointing), or by understanding metaphorical uses. Examples: Hippias' defenses of Homer via accent or pointing changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge a thing in context: speaker, addressee, time, means, and end
rubrics_metrics.description: To know whether a thing be well or ill done or spoken, we must not be satisfied to examine the thing itself, but we must also have respect to him who speaks, or acts, and to him to whom he addresses himself, and to consider well the Time, the Means, and the End.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate utterances/actions according to who says them, to whom, at what time, with what means, and to what purpose — many things that seem wrong in isolation are justified in context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absurdities/impossibilities may be pardoned if they secure poetic verisimilitude or wonder
rubrics_metrics.description: The Poet is guilty of a Fault beyond Contradiction, if he advances those things which are impossible according to the Rules of his Art. But this ceases to be a fault, when by those means he obtains the end which he proposed (e.g., to excite wonder).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Probable-impossible (things that serve verisimilitude or produce admiring wonder) can be preferable to merely possible but incredible details; still, avoid unnecessary violations of art if the same effect can be achieved without them. Example: Achilles pursuing Hector; Ulysses left asleep—absurdities used to heighten effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify objections into five heads
rubrics_metrics.description: Objections to poets may be reduced under five heads: for they may be blamed for saying things which are either impossible, or absurd, or bad, or which contradict one another, or are contrary to the Rules of Art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When answering critics, sort the complaint into one of these categories and apply the appropriate line of defense (modes of imitation, diction liberties, appeal to custom, rhetorical devices, or demonstration that fault is accidental).

rubrics_metrics.name: When diction seems wrong, examine all possible senses of the word
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever a Word seems to signify something contrary to the Intention of the Poet, we should examine all the different Significations which the Word can have in the Passage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many apparent errors are semantic: words have multiple meanings or usages (e.g., Greek examples: a word translated 'mules' may mean 'guards' or 'sentinels'); choose the meaning that fits context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconcile apparent contradictions by logical examination
rubrics_metrics.description: As for those things which seem contrary to what has been said before, we must examine them as we do Objections in Logic: that is to say we must enquire whether it be the same thing, tend to the same end, and whether it be spoken in the same manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check identity of referent, purpose, and mode of speaking; differences in speaker or rhetorical aim can explain seeming inconsistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer imaginative strength over pedantry; ignorance of facts less blameworthy than bad imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: We may more voluntarily excuse that Poet, who does not know, that a Doe has Horns, than he who shall make a bad Imitation... nothing is more disagreeable than a Poet who affects to shew an Universal Knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minor factual errors due to ignorance (forests, animals, local facts) are more pardonable than failures in the poet's own art (bad imitation). Avoid pedantic displays of encyclopedic knowledge which harm poetic effect.
